Interdiction de filmer dans les hôpitaux: Hospital filming bans: a measure that undermines Indigenous people’s sense of safety
Pour M. Joseph et sa conjointe, l’affich: For Mr. Joseph and his partner, the sign is a provocation.
« Afin de respecter la vie privée, la pr: “To respect privacy, taking photographs or shooting videos showing a patient or a staff member without their knowledge is prohibited, for anyone.”
C’est ce qu’on peut lire sur une affiche: That is what a sign reads in the intensive care unit of the CISSS de Lanaudière, where Joyce Echaquan lost her life on September 28. It is a sign that reopens wounds, as the tragedy remains very present in the memory of members of Indigenous communities in Quebec.
Cela fait maintenant six mois que Joyce: It has now been six months since Joyce Echaquan livestreamed her final moments on her phone.
C’est son tournage, en infraction à cett: It was her filming, in breach of this directive, that allowed the whole world to see and hear a reality that many Indigenous people experience in the health-care system. A photo of the sign made the rounds on social media last December. Carol Dubé, Joyce’s husband, was struck by it. He called the Joliette hospital to understand the reason for the directive. “They say it’s been there since 2018, but I never saw it,” he tells us.
Après la mort de Joyce Echaquan, les int: After Joyce Echaquan’s death, bans on filming in hospitals are shocking many people in Indigenous communities. Adélard Joseph, an Innu-aimun teacher, accompanied his wife to the Sept-Îles hospital for an appointment last December. “At registration, right next to it, there was a wall with a sign that said not to take photos or videos,” he explains, adding that he had never seen such a sign at the hospital before.
Pour M. Joseph et sa conjointe, l’affich: For Mr. Joseph and his partner, the sign is a provocation. “Right away, in my head, it made me think of the Joyce Echaquan case; it really got to me,” he continues. “My wife felt frustrated. It got to her too.”
“I didn’t know Joyce Echaquan. I know she was Atikamekw. She was an Indigenous woman. She wanted services. Seeing a nurse insulting an Indigenous patient, it made me react, it got to me deep inside. Has this happened before? Yes, but we didn’t have cellphones or proof.”
Aujourd’hui, il accompagne sa conjointe: Today, he accompanies his partner to every one of her hospital visits to reassure her. “It could happen again,” Mr. Joseph says, alluding to Joyce Echaquan’s death and the racism she experienced at the hospital.
Ce couple exprime non seulement sa frust: The couple is expressing not only their frustration with the signs, but also the need to strengthen cultural safety for Indigenous people in Quebec’s hospitals.
Sipi Flamand témoigne de la méfiance de: Sipi Flamand speaks to the Manawan community’s mistrust of health care at the Joliette hospital. “I also understand that the presence of that sign is necessary, but with Joyce’s story, I think the CIUSSS, the Lanaudière social services centre and the others need to consider another approach, because we can see that families are a bit more wary of the hospital,” explains the vice-chief of the Conseil des Atikamekw de Manawan.
Sipi Flamand demande des explications au: Sipi Flamand is asking for explanations about the relevance of the signs. “I think they should review them. And really explain why those signs were put up,” he adds. While using a cellphone is prohibited in certain areas of hospitals for safety reasons, Grand Chief of the Atikamekw Nation Constant Awashish also questions the relevance of these signs at the Joliette hospital. “The use of the sign has to be justified. In the current context, I don’t think it’s justifiable,” he says. Sandrine Filiatrault, a medical trainee from the Wendat Nation, believes the directives banning filming in hospitals have their reasons, but need to be reviewed.
« C’est totalement inadéquat de prendre: “It’s completely inappropriate to take videos and photos of others without their permission, even more so if they’re in a vulnerable situation in hospital while they’re sick,” she says. “However, I think you have to use your judgment, and each case deserves to be assessed separately,” adds the future doctor.
« Dans le cas de Joyce, on comprend clai: “In Joyce’s case, it’s clear that the primary purpose of her video wasn’t to violate anyone’s privacy, but rather to denounce a completely unacceptable situation. In cases like this, taking into account the concepts of systemic racism and cultural safety, in my view, this rule shouldn’t apply,” <l1>Sandrine Filiatrault</l1> believes. Indigenous Affairs Minister Ian Lafrenière was not aware of the signs or the unease they were causing in communities before our call. “I hope there’s no connection with what happened with Ms. Echaquan,” he tells us over the phone. He adds that he is curious and disappointed. “Honestly, I would be furious to learn that the signs were put up after the events.”
Nous l’informons que, d’après le CIUSSS: We inform him that, according to the CIUSSS de Lanaudière, they have been in place since 2018 in various facilities, with the aim of ensuring respect for the privacy of patients and hospital staff. The CISSS de Lanaudière informed us by email that it has taken note of this concern from community members and will follow up with its cultural safety officer. But there was no answer as to whether the CISSS will add context to the sign.
« On parle de quelque chose qui était là: “We’re talking about something that was there before, but I fully understand the sensitivity,” adds the Minister Responsible for Indigenous Affairs, who assures us he will follow up with the hospital. Several people we interviewed say they had not seen this kind of directive in hospitals before Joyce Echaquan’s death. The CISSS de Lanaudière confirms, however, that it has not put up any more signs in recent months. As for the CISSS de la Côte-Nord, which oversees the Sept-Îles hospital, last month it updated its signs, which dated back several years, to add video recording in addition to photos.
Cette mise à jour était nécessaire, dit: This update was necessary, the institution says. The first sign was created on its own initiative several years ago and is posted notably in emergency rooms, communications and legal affairs adviser Marlène Joseph-Blais tells us. According to the Ministry of Health and Social Services, these signs are not unique to the CISSS de Lanaudière and the CISSS de la Côte-Nord.
Elles ne relèvent toutefois pas de direc: They do not, however, stem from provincial directives. They stem from the right to privacy, which is protected in Quebec under the Civil Code and the Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms.
Mais pourquoi ces directives sont-elles: But why are these directives relevant? According to Patrick Martin-Ménard, a lawyer specializing in health issues, the directives are based on the right to confidentiality of patients and staff in hospital settings. “As far as patients go, I think it’s clear,” he tells us. “In my view, there’s little room for debate. Every patient has the right to the confidentiality of their medical record.”
« Maintenant, il y a un autre élément, q: “Now, there’s another element, which is the staff,” continues the lawyer, whose firm is dedicated to defending the rights of patients harmed by the health-care system. “Often, in the past, there have been cases where staff were filmed without their knowledge, and that led to public denunciations with videos published in which staff were clearly identifiable. And in some cases, it had negative consequences for them.”
Me Martin-Ménard note toutefois un vide: Martin-Ménard notes, however, a legislative void regarding this right to confidentiality and a lack of uniformity in the directive. “There’s reason to find a way to legislate so that videos can be filmed in a context that both respects patients’ confidentiality requirements and makes it possible to document situations that may prove problematic.” According to him, each institution adopts its own rules to enforce the right to confidentiality.
Un droit appliqué de façon variable d’un: It is a right applied inconsistently from one place to another, as the Ministry of Health and Social Services confirms to us. In some places, these directives are strictly enforced, and in others, patients have been able to film the care they received in detail without having their phones taken away, Martin-Ménard reports.
Le vide législatif déclenche plusieurs p: The legislative void is a trigger for many people, especially after Joyce Echaquan’s death, as the people we spoke with attest. The Public Inquiry Commission on relations between Indigenous Peoples and certain public services in Quebec showed that the quality of services offered to Indigenous peoples has never been a priority.
Nous discutons donc des affiches avec le: So we discuss the signs with the co-director of research for the Viens Commission. “When, spontaneously, you look at a sign whose basic objective is to protect people’s privacy, but in the end it’s interpreted as endangering those people’s lives, it’s because, somewhere, there’s a message that isn’t getting through,” says Sébastien Brodeur-Girard, co-director of research for the Viens Commission and professor at UQAT’s School of Indigenous Studies.
Mais c’est grâce au téléphone de Joyce E: But it was thanks to Joyce Echaquan’s phone that the message about the realities Indigenous peoples experience in Quebec institutions got through. As several Indigenous experts attest, it was indeed after Joyce Echaquan’s death that the Viens Commission’s 142 recommendations began to be implemented more seriously.
« Si Joyce ne s’était pas filmée, on n’e: “If Joyce hadn’t filmed herself, we wouldn’t have heard about it. And that’s an awareness that has to follow as well. Because, yes, people were shocked by the existence of this discrimination, but beyond that, we have to realize that this discrimination exists and it’s continuing. We don’t pay attention to it, because it has to be filmed for people to realize something is happening. It takes images, otherwise it always gets brushed aside. That’s a serious issue.”
<strong>Le principe de Joyce pour répare: Joyce’s Principle as a path to repair
D’après les gens que nous avons consulté: According to the people we consulted, the signs banning filming in hospitals undermine cultural safety for Indigenous people. There is still an enormous way to go to repair relations between Indigenous communities and the health-care system. Joyce’s Principle proposes a step in that direction.
« Avec le principe de Joyce, on propose: “With Joyce’s Principle, we’re proposing to work together to find ways to raise awareness,” says Sipi Flamand, vice-chief of the Manawan community. “I think the Joliette hospital and other hospitals could reach out to begin a collaboration with Indigenous communities and see how they could raise awareness, whether about reconciliation or about healing together, between Indigenous communities and hospitals.”
Ce principe tarde toutefois à être appli: The provincial government, however, has been slow to apply this principle. “We didn’t agree on systemic racism,” Minister Responsible for Indigenous Affairs Ian Lafrenière tells us. “But even if we didn’t agree on the principle of systemic racism, that doesn’t stop us from fighting racism. We’re partly responding to Joyce’s Principle,” he says, referring to the appointment of a member of the Manawan community to the board of directors of the CISSS de Lanaudière.
En attendant, à l’hôpital de Joliette, o: In the meantime, at the Joliette hospital, where Joyce Echaquan lost her life moments after filming herself being subjected to racist insults by members of the care staff, signs prohibiting what she did remain up without any context.
